```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A course coordinator sends you a survey spreadsheet. Before comparing the
centres, you need to understand its columns, clean its measurements and check
that the records fit together. This guide introduces that workflow; each
function's reference page covers its additional options.

## Find your way around

Here are the twelve participants from [Getting started](getting-started.html).
The two scores are assessment items, and `-99` means income was undisclosed.

```{r survey, message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(tidystata)

survey <- tribble(
  ~id, ~centre,     ~satisfied, ~income_text, ~score1, ~score2,
    1, "Riverside", "Yes",     "1,200",           2,       4,
    2, "Riverside", "Yes",     "1,500",           4,      NA,
    3, "Riverside", "No",      "",               NA,      NA,
    4, "Riverside", NA,        "-99",             6,       8,
    5, "Riverside", "Yes",     "2,200",           8,      10,
    6, "Riverside", "Yes",     "1,800",           4,       6,
    7, "Hilltop",   "No",      "1,400",           3,       5,
    8, "Hilltop",   "Yes",     "2,100",           5,       7,
    9, "Hilltop",   "No",      "2,600",           7,       9,
   10, "Hilltop",   "Yes",     NA,                9,      NA,
   11, "Hilltop",   "Yes",     "2,300",          NA,       8,
   12, "Hilltop",   NA,        "1,700",           6,       8
) |>
  mutate(score1 = haven::labelled(score1, label = "First assessment item"))

survey |> variables()
```

`variables()` pairs column names with their labels. Search the descriptions
when a large file has names that are hard to remember:

```{r search}
survey |> variables_search("assessment")
```

Use `ds()` for a vector of matching names, or `codebook()` for types and counts.
The same tidy selection works when inspecting or calculating:

```{r select}
survey |>
  select_or_transmute(id, starts_with("score"), income = destring(income_text))
```

`select_or_transmute()` combines selecting existing columns and computing new
ones. `varlist("score*")` offers Stata-style wildcard selection; ordinary
`starts_with()` works throughout this guide. For an interactive spreadsheet
view, use `browse()` in your own session.

## Clean values before calculating

Read the income strings and replace the sentinel. Use `across()` to apply a
conversion to several columns when needed.

```{r clean}
clean <- survey |>
  mutate(income = destring(income_text) |> mvdecode(-99))

clean |> misstable(income, starts_with("score"))
```

The income column now has three missing values: a blank answer, the sentinel
and an original `NA`. Use `na_if_value()` for the corresponding single-value
replacement. `mvencode()` and `value_if_na()` go in the other direction when an
export needs a sentinel; keep ordinary `NA` values for calculations.

Category codes need a different decision. `encode()` gives text categories
labelled integer codes. `decode()` reads those labels back; `tostring()` and
its alias `as_character()` instead return the stored codes as text.

```{r categories}
clean |>
  mutate(
    centre_code = encode(centre),
    centre_label = decode(centre_code),
    code_text = tostring(centre_code)
  ) |>
  distinct(centre, centre_code, centre_label, code_text)
```

Encode before grouping so all centres share one coding dictionary. Keep exact
identifiers as text from import, rather than converting rounded numbers back
to strings.

## Create measurements inside `mutate()`

How many assessment items did each participant answer, and what was their
average? Row helpers work directly with the columns selected by `pick()`.

```{r scores}
prepared <- clean |>
  mutate(
    score = row_mean(pick(score1, score2)),
    answered = row_non_miss(pick(score1, score2)),
    score_z = std(score)
  )

prepared |> select(id, starts_with("score"), answered)
```

The all-missing participant keeps an `NA` average. `std()` expresses the
observed averages in sample standard deviations. Related row helpers calculate
sums, minima, maxima and missing counts without a `rowwise()` step.

For a simple reporting band, recode ranges and then display their labels:

```{r bands}
prepared |>
  mutate(band = stata_recode(score, Lower = min:5 ~ 1, Higher = 5:max ~ 2)) |>
  fre(band)
```

Rules are applied in order, so a score of exactly 5 belongs to Lower.
`xtile()` makes quantile groups while keeping ties together; `cut_breaks()`
uses chosen boundaries and `cut_length()` equal-width intervals. For indicator
columns, use `as_dummy()` (also called `tab_gen()`); its `.names` option selects
value-, index- or label-based names.

## Check records before combining them

A participant ID should identify one survey row. `isid()` confirms the key
and passes the data along; `assert()` checks a condition inside the pipeline.

```{r checks}
prepared |>
  isid(id) |>
  assert(is.na(score) | (score >= 0 & score <= 10)) |>
  select(id, score) |>
  print_headtail(n = 4)
```

If an import contains repeated records, start with `duplicates_report()` and
inspect them with `duplicates_list()`. `duplicates_tag()` marks them, and
`duplicates_drop()` keeps the first after you decide which rows are redundant.

Now attach the number of course sessions offered by each centre. Declare the
many-participants-to-one-centre relationship and require a match for every row.

```{r merge}
centres <- tribble(
  ~centre,     ~sessions,
  "Riverside",         8,
  "Hilltop",          10
)

prepared |>
  stata_merge(centres, "m:1", by = "centre", assert = "match") |>
  select(id, centre, sessions, .merge) |>
  print_headtail(n = 4)
```

The `.merge` column records match status. Use dplyr joins for ordinary joins;
`stata_merge()` is useful when you also want Stata-style match reporting and
checks.

## Follow participants over time

A later survey creates a panel. Participant 1 misses wave 2: the change from
the previous wave should therefore be missing at wave 3.

```{r panel}
followup <- tribble(
  ~id, ~wave, ~score,
    1,     1,      3,
    1,     3,      7,
    2,     1,      4,
    2,     2,      6
)

followup |>
  isid(id, wave) |>
  mutate(
    previous = stata_lag(score, time = wave),
    change = stata_diff(score, time = wave),
    .by = id
  )
```

These helpers find the previous *period*, whereas `dplyr::lag()` finds the
previous row. `stata_lead()` looks ahead by period. Always identify the panel
in `.by` or `group_by()`.

## Keep exploring

Use [category tables](tabulation.html) to compare responses and
[measurement summaries](summary-statistics.html) to compare scores and incomes.
`preview()` controls a table's continuing display, while `print_headtail()`
and `print_interval()` print it briefly once; all retain the complete data.
See the [conventions guide](containers-and-missing-values.html) for details.

For occasional workflow tasks, the reference covers reproducible draws with
`set_seed()`, timing with `timer()`, and continuing after an optional expression
fails with `capture()`. To find a familiar Stata operation, try
`findit("tab satisfied")`; editor and clipboard helpers are also available.
